title: 年轻人为何重拾修理技能
paragraphs: When the screen of Chen Yu's laptop began to flicker last spring, her first thought was to replace it. The second-year economics student was already comparing prices online when a classmate mentioned a free repair event held every month in the university library. Two hours later, with the help of a volunteer and a tiny screwdriver, she found that the problem was nothing more than a loose cable. "I felt a little silly at first," she admits, "but mostly I felt proud. I had no idea I was capable of fixing anything."

Chen is one of a growing number of young people who are rediscovering the old habit of mending things instead of throwing them away. Repair events like the one she attended have been appearing in cities and college towns around the world. They are usually organized by volunteers and held in community centers, libraries or cafés. Visitors bring broken lamps, torn jackets, bicycles with flat tires and phones that refuse to charge, and they sit down beside someone who knows how to fix them.

Not long ago, such skills were simply part of everyday life. Many of today's grandparents grew up darning socks, replacing the soles of their shoes and taking apart radios on the kitchen table. Things were expensive compared with wages, so people made them last. As factories began to produce goods more cheaply, however, buying something new often became easier than repairing the old one. Over a few decades, a culture of fixing gave way to a culture of replacing.

Manufacturers have also made repair harder. Many modern devices are held together with glue rather than screws, or with unusual screws that ordinary tools cannot turn. Batteries are often sealed inside, and spare parts can be difficult or impossible to buy. Some companies do not publish repair manuals at all, which means that even a skilled person may have to guess how a machine is put together. "Sometimes the hardest part is just getting the case open," says one volunteer who has fixed electronics for more than twenty years.

Supporters of the repair movement argue that this throwaway habit has a heavy environmental cost. Every phone, kettle and washing machine requires metals, plastics and energy to produce, and most of that is lost when the product ends up in a landfill. Electronic waste is especially worrying because it can contain substances that harm soil and water if they are not handled properly. Keeping a device in use for even one or two extra years, they say, means fewer new ones need to be made.

For many students, though, the most immediate reason to learn repair is money. Living on a tight budget, they cannot afford to replace a broken phone or bicycle whenever something goes wrong. Liu Hao, a graduate student who now volunteers at a repair event in his city, says he first came because he could not pay for a new bike. "A new chain cost me a tiny fraction of the price of a new bicycle," he says. "After that, I started asking what else I could fix myself."

The benefits are not only practical. Many people find that solving a concrete problem with their own hands gives them a strong sense of achievement. Repairing something requires patience, careful observation and a willingness to try again after a mistake, and these are qualities that can be hard to develop in front of a screen. A number of young people say that fixing an object for the first time made them feel more confident about dealing with problems in other areas of their lives.

Repair events also bring together people who might otherwise never meet. Retired engineers and tailors sit at the same table as teenagers and university students, and the conversation often goes far beyond the broken object. "The older volunteers have so much knowledge, and they love sharing it," says Chen, who now helps out at the library event herself. For some elderly volunteers, the events offer a welcome chance to feel useful and to stay connected with their neighborhood.

Of course, many young people learn their first repair skills not from a person but from the internet. Online videos show how to replace a cracked screen or sew on a button, step by step. Yet volunteers point out that videos have limits. They cannot see your particular machine, warn you when you are about to damage something, or answer the question you did not know to ask. That is why many beginners use online tutorials to prepare and then bring their questions to a repair event.

There are signs that businesses and governments are beginning to respond. In some places, new rules require manufacturers to make spare parts available for a number of years after a product is sold. A few companies have started selling repair kits and publishing guides for their customers, partly because they have noticed that buyers increasingly care about how long a product will last. Some schools, too, have brought back basic repair lessons as part of their practical education courses.

Not everyone is convinced that repair is always the right choice. Some critics point out that an old appliance may use far more electricity than a new, efficient model, so keeping it running is not necessarily better for the environment. Others warn that opening certain devices, especially those with large batteries, can be dangerous without proper training. And for busy people, spending an afternoon fixing a cheap item may simply not seem worth the time.

Even so, those involved in the movement believe that something important is changing. Chen Yu says the biggest difference is in how she looks at the things she owns. "Before, when something broke, I thought it was finished," she says. "Now my first question is: can this be saved?" For a generation that grew up surrounded by cheap and easily replaced goods, that small question may turn out to be a big step.

title: 让被掩埋的城市河流重见天日
topic: urban rivers, daylighting, environment, city planning
paragraphs: For most of the past century, residents of one old district in a large Asian city had no idea there was a river beneath their feet. A four-lane road and a row of parking lots covered the channel, and the only sign of the water was a faint smell that rose from the drains on hot summer evenings. Today the road is gone. In its place is a narrow, shallow stream lined with reeds and stepping stones, where office workers eat lunch and children chase small fish. The transformation took nearly ten years, and it was far from simple.

The story of how the stream disappeared is a common one. During the rapid growth of industrial cities in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, small rivers were often treated as little more than open sewers. They carried household waste and factory runoff, they smelled terrible, and they were blamed, sometimes correctly, for outbreaks of disease. Covering them over seemed an obvious solution. It removed an unpleasant sight and created valuable flat land for roads, railways and buildings at a time when space in city centers was increasingly scarce.

What engineers of that era could not fully foresee were the long-term costs. A river forced into a pipe or concrete tunnel can carry only a fixed amount of water. When heavy storms arrive, as they do with growing frequency in many regions, these underground channels can overflow, flooding streets and basements. The tunnels themselves also age. Many that were built a hundred years ago are now crumbling, and repairing or replacing them can cost city governments enormous sums, often for infrastructure that no one ever sees.

Against this background, a growing number of cities have begun to consider what planners call "daylighting": removing the covering from a buried waterway and allowing it to flow in the open once again. The term covers a wide range of projects. At one end are ambitious restorations that try to recreate a natural riverbed, with curving banks, gravel and native plants. At the other are more modest designs in which water runs through a stone or concrete channel that is clearly artificial but at least visible to the public.

Ecologists are among the strongest supporters of the idea. A stream that sits in permanent darkness supports very little life, but once it is exposed to sunlight, algae and water plants begin to grow, and these in turn attract insects, fish and birds. In several reopened streams, species that had not been recorded in the area for decades have reappeared within a few years. Even a narrow strip of open water, researchers note, can serve as a corridor that allows wildlife to move between parks that would otherwise be isolated from one another.

There are climate benefits as well. Cities tend to be noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside, because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Open water and the vegetation that grows beside it can lower temperatures in the immediate area, especially on the hottest days of summer. For residents of crowded neighborhoods with few trees, the difference can be more than a matter of comfort; during heat waves, it may reduce health risks for elderly people and young children.

The economic effects are more complicated. Reopened streams often become popular places to walk, and the streets around them can attract new cafés, shops and visitors. Property values nearby frequently rise. For homeowners, this is welcome news, but for tenants it can mean higher rents. In some cities, long-time residents and small businesses have been gradually pushed out of the very neighborhoods that were improved, a process critics describe as "green gentrification." Planners increasingly argue that daylighting projects should be paired with policies that protect affordable housing.

The practical obstacles are considerable too. Beneath most city streets lies a dense tangle of water pipes, gas lines and electrical cables, all of which may have to be moved before a stream can be uncovered. The land above a buried river is frequently owned by many different parties, and negotiating with each of them takes time. Water quality is another concern: if sewage still leaks into the channel, opening it up may simply expose the public to the very problems that led to its burial in the first place.

Some critics question whether the money is well spent. They point out that the same budget could build several new schools or improve public transport, which might benefit far more people. Others complain that certain projects are more about appearance than ecology. In some cases, the "river" that visitors admire is largely pumped in from elsewhere and treated with chemicals, making it closer to a long fountain than a living stream. Such projects, critics argue, risk giving daylighting a reputation it does not deserve.

Where daylighting has worked best, local communities have usually been involved from the beginning. In one mid-sized European city, residents spent several years debating the design of their reopened stream at public meetings before construction began. Afterwards, volunteer groups took responsibility for clearing litter and planting along the banks, while local schools adopted sections of the stream for science lessons, with pupils regularly testing the water and recording the animals they found. Such involvement, organizers say, gives people a sense of ownership that makes a project far more likely to last.

Researchers have also become interested in the effect that urban water has on people's minds. Being near water, whether it is the sea, a lake or a small stream, appears to help many people feel calmer, and the gentle sound of moving water can mask some of the noise of traffic. In surveys, residents living close to reopened streams often say they spend more time outdoors and talk more with their neighbors. While such findings do not prove that the streams themselves are the cause, they suggest that the benefits may extend well beyond the environment.

None of this means that every buried river should be brought back to the surface. In some places the costs are simply too high, and in others there is no realistic way to move the roads and buildings that now sit on top of the water. But the growing interest in daylighting reflects a broader shift in how cities think about nature. For generations, urban rivers were seen as problems to be hidden away. Increasingly, they are being seen as assets: features that can make cities cooler, greener and more pleasant places to live.
